title: Why Custom Commands Merged Into Skills

questions.prompt: Your team's release command lives in .claude/commands/release.md and has worked for a year. Which statement about it is actually true today?
options: It still runs as /release, but name and paths in its frontmatter are not honoured — skills accept those two fields, command files do not
It still runs as /release, but it is deprecated and will stop loading on the next major version
It no longer loads at all; use .claude/skills/release/SKILL.md instead or the command disappears
It still runs as /release, but the model can now auto-invoke it from its description, which it could never do before
questions.explanation: The merge is equivalence plus supersession: legacy files keep working, and the two fields they lack are name and paths. Option B overclaims — the docs describe a soft direction with backward compatibility and no removal notice. Option C is the failure mode people actually fear and it is not what shipped; existing .claude/commands files continue to work. Option D inverts the capability: automatic, description-matched invocation is one of the things skills add, so a command file still cannot do it.

questions.prompt: Your deploy command needs to run ./scripts/preflight.sh before deploying, and the script already exists next to the project root. What is the actual blocker with keeping the command file?
options: Command files cannot invoke scripts at all, so this has to become a hook
The script path would be relative to the wrong file, since a command's frontmatter has no working-directory field
A command file is a single .md — it has no folder to hold or reference a sibling script, which is exactly what the skill directory restores
Nothing blocks it — the command can just inline the shell command instead of calling the script
questions.explanation: The blocker is structural, not behavioural: a command is one markdown blob, so the skill's directory is what lets supporting files travel with the instructions. Option A reaches for hooks, which are a different phase and would be the wrong tool for a per-invocation precondition. Option B invents a field that does not exist. Option D is tempting and wrong in practice — inlining the script body duplicates logic that already has a home, and it is precisely the drift the docs warn about when they describe shipping scripts with skills.

questions.prompt: You have 14 legacy command files across a repo. What is the honest migration posture?
options: Migrate all 14 now — anything in .claude/commands/ is second-class and will rot
Migrate none — the folder format is deprecated and skills are a separate product
Migrate on contact: convert a file when it needs a folder, a trigger rule, or a teammate to receive it; leave the rest
Migrate only the ones with under 30 lines, since short prompts have the most to gain from fields
questions.explanation: Migrate-on-contact is the posture that matches the docs: new work prefers skills, existing files work fine, and each of the four added capabilities is a concrete trigger for converting one specific file. Option A treats working files as rot and spends a rename across 14 files for no gain. Option B inverts the direction — skills are where the format is heading, not commands. Option D is arbitrary; nothing about prompt length determines which fields you can use.
